articles.title: 'Big Bang' Fix Puts Voyager Across the 'One Light-Day' Mark
articles.description: Flashback to 1977. Jimmy Carter was U.S. president, Star Wars was a box office hit, and the two Voyager spacecraft departed on an historic Grand Tour of the solar system. Now, teams at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory are working to keep the missions active, as they push the boundaries of interstellar space beyond the solar system.
articles.summary: The legendary Voyager spacecraft, launched in 1977, has crossed the one light-day distance milestone in its historic interstellar journey.

articles.title: NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera is closing in to see what happened
articles.description: Europe’s Hera spacecraft has captured its first clear view of two asteroids involved in NASA’s historic 2022 experiment to redirect a potentially dangerous space rock. Now approaching the pair, Hera will investigate the mysterious aftermath of the collision and uncover why the asteroid shifted far more than scientists predicted.
articles.summary: Europe's Hera spacecraft has captured detailed imagery of the asteroids involved in NASA's groundbreaking DART kinetic impact experiment, analyzing the historic mission's results.

articles.title: All 5 genetic “letters” of DNA and RNA discovered in a 4.5-billion-year-old asteroid
articles.description: Scientists have discovered all five essential nucleobases used in DNA and RNA in pristine samples from asteroid Ryugu, revealing that key ingredients for life existed in space billions of years ago. The remarkable finding adds to growing evidence from other asteroids and meteorites that these molecules were widespread throughout the early Solar System.
articles.summary: Scientists discovered all five nucleobases of DNA and RNA in pristine samples from asteroid Ryugu, suggesting the building blocks of life may have extraterrestrial origins. This landmark finding from a sample-return mission deepens our understanding of how life's chemistry emerged in the cosmos.

articles.title: M30’s Sparkling Stars
articles.description: This NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope image released Nov. 5, 2026, provides a lesson in galactic history. The sparkling collection of stars is named Messier 30 (M30) after the French astronomer, Charles Messier, who cataloged M30 and other diffuse objects that might be mistaken for comets in the early telescopes of Messier’s time. M30 lies about […]
articles.summary: NASA/ESA's Hubble Space Telescope captured a stunning image of M30 revealing sparkling stars that offer insights into galactic history and stellar evolution.

articles.title: Hubble Learns Galactic History From Stars
articles.description: This Hubble image features the sparkling collection of stars named Messier 30 (M30), also called NGC 7099.
articles.summary: Hubble reveals the stellar collection of Messier 30 (NGC 7099), showcasing sparkling stars that illuminate galactic history and formation mechanisms.

articles.title: The ELT Can Probe Ultra-Diffuse Galaxies and Their Dark Matter Mysteries
articles.description: Ultra-Diffuse Galaxies are strange because they're as large as the Milky Way, but have far fewer stars. It's as if they're puffed up for some reason. Determining what's going on with them could help confirm the Lambda-CDM model. A new proposed instrument for the Extremely Large Telescope could give astronomers their best look yet at these strange galaxies.
articles.summary: The Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) will probe ultra-diffuse galaxies to unlock dark matter mysteries and understand why these galactic giants contain so few stars.

articles.title: NASA's Twin Spacecraft Will Execute Powered Slingshot Maneuvers on Their Way to Mars
articles.description: NASA's ESCAPADE mission features a pair of identical spacecraft on their way to Mars. They launched outside of the normal launch window, so they'll perform powered slingshot maneuvers to boost their speed. Once there, they'll "fly" in formation and study how the solar wind interacts with what remains of Mars ancient magnetosphere.
articles.summary: NASA's ESCAPADE mission features twin spacecraft executing innovative powered slingshot maneuvers on their groundbreaking journey to Mars.

articles.title: A Mighty Wind Blew Away Gas and Made Early Galaxies Brighter
articles.description: When astronomers looked at photos of the early universe taken by the James Webb Space Telescope, they found something odd: an overabundance of bright galaxies about 400 to 500 million years after the Big Bang. But these galaxies should have been far less common so soon after the Big Bang. Researchers may have figured this out: Powerful ultraviolet (Lyman-alpha) radiation produced by dense clusters of young stars acted like a leaf blower, driving light-blocking gas and dust out of the galaxy and thereby making the galaxies appear brighter.
articles.summary: James Webb Space Telescope observations reveal that powerful winds cleared gas from early galaxies, making them brighter and transforming our understanding of cosmic dawn.

articles.title: Interstellar Visitor 3I/ATLAS Shows Water Ice Behaves the Same Across Alien Star Systems
articles.description: Targets of opportunity sometimes happen in astronomy, and we got a major one when the third interstellar object, 3I/ATLAS, was discovered in July 2025. And it just so happens that in the intervening years between the last known interstellar visitor (2I/Borisov in 2019), we got a major upgrade in our observational capabilities with the launch of the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). A new paper from a team of researchers led by Dr. Silvia Protopapa of NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center and the Southwest Research Institute, and published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, details JWST’s findings on the water ice content of this most recent visitor from beyond our solar system.
articles.summary: The interstellar visitor 3I/ATLAS provides remarkable insights showing that water ice behaves consistently across different star systems.

articles.title: Exoplanets Can't Hide From The JWST's 'Digital Twin'
articles.description: Finding dim exoplanets hidden in the glare of their stars is an ongoing challenge in astronomy. Telescopes use coronagraphs to block out starlight, but even they have their limitations. Researchers have developed a new technique with the JWST that can find dim exoplanets more easily than ever.
articles.summary: The JWST's advanced digital twin technology enables astronomers to detect dim exoplanets obscured by stellar glare, overcoming a major challenge in exoplanet discovery.

articles.title: Vibrating mirrors of light create analog of a black hole event horizon
articles.description: Optical cavities are pairs of light-trapping mirrors and underpin the operation of lasers, atomic clocks and many types of precision sensors. If the distance between the mirrors is changed rapidly enough, some theories predict that the waves inside them should bunch together into short, intense pulses. So far, however, this prediction has never been tested directly.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Researchers have created an optical analog of a black hole event horizon using vibrating mirrors of light, advancing our understanding of black hole physics through laboratory experimentation.

articles.title: Robot successfully builds space structure in first autonomous construction demo
articles.description: A robotic truss builder that was conceived, designed and built by Caltech researchers has successfully built a structure in space—without the help of astronauts—for the first time. The truss builder, part of DARPA's Novel Orbital and Moon Manufacturing, Materials, and Mass-efficient Design (NOM4D) program, consists of an autonomous manipulator that picks up struts and joints held in nearby dispensers to repeatedly assemble identical sections, or bays, of a perimeter truss.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Caltech engineers have demonstrated the first successful autonomous construction of a space structure using a robotic truss builder, paving the way for future in-space manufacturing.

articles.title: A galaxy nicknamed Misty Moons offers a glimpse of early star formation
articles.description: Gravitational lensing is one of astronomy's best tricks for seeing the early universe. When a massive galaxy cluster sits in between the observer and a distant object, its gravity bends and magnifies the distant object's light, acting like a giant natural magnifying glass. Galaxies that would otherwise be too faint to spot suddenly come into view because of gravitational lensing.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: The galaxy 'Misty Moons' provides unprecedented insight into early star formation through gravitational lensing, offering a window into the universe's distant past.

articles.title: Astronomers deliver the sharpest and deepest view yet of the low-frequency radio sky
articles.description: Using the Low Frequency Array (LOFAR), an international team led by Leiden University has produced the sharpest and most sensitive radio image of the sky ever made at low radio frequencies. The image reveals almost 63,000 radio sources, such as active galactic nuclei and star-forming galaxies, across a patch of sky about 25 times the area of the full moon. The results have been accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics. The paper is currently available on the arXiv preprint server.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: The Low Frequency Array (LOFAR) has captured the sharpest and deepest view of the low-frequency radio sky to date, revealing new details across the universe.

articles.title: NASA’s Voyager 1 is about to reach a historic one-light-day milestone
articles.description: NASA’s Voyager 1 is approaching an extraordinary milestone nearly 50 years after its launch, even as engineers battle dwindling power and mysterious technical problems. A clever energy-saving maneuver has extended the spacecraft’s scientific mission, while an unexplained 48-hour communications blackout recently gave NASA a scare. On November 18, Voyager 1 will reach a distance of one light-day from Earth, making even the simplest round-trip communication take 48 hours.
articles.summary: NASA's Voyager 1 is approaching a historic one-light-day milestone nearly 50 years after launch, continuing its remarkable journey through deep space.

articles.title: A hidden star is plowing through Betelgeuse’s atmosphere, new evidence suggests
articles.description: Something mysterious is disturbing Betelgeuse, and astronomers believe they have identified the culprit: a hidden companion star called Siwarha. New radio observations reveal that the smaller star may be plowing through Betelgeuse’s enormous atmosphere, creating disturbances that subtly stretch and distort the red supergiant’s shape.
articles.summary: Astronomers have discovered evidence of a hidden companion star plowing through Betelgeuse's atmosphere, explaining mysterious disturbances in this famous red supergiant.

articles.title: Dead stars could break one of physics' most famous limits
articles.description: A surprising new discovery suggests that some dead stars can grow far more massive than scientists once thought possible. Computer simulations show that powerful magnetic fields could allow white dwarfs to reach 2.4 times the mass of the Sun, dramatically exceeding a famous limit that has stood for decades. The findings could help explain unusually bright supernova explosions that have long puzzled astronomers.
articles.summary: New research reveals that neutron stars can achieve significantly greater masses than previously thought possible, challenging fundamental limits in physics.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 6, 1572: A German astronomer discovers the Tycho supernova with the naked eye, but everyone thought the cosmic explosion was a 'new star'
articles.description: On Nov. 6, 1572, the German astronomer Wolfgang Schulër observed a supernova later caleld the Tycho supernova with his bare eyes. Here's why it mattered.
articles.summary: On November 6, 1572, German astronomer Wolfgang Schuler observed the Tycho supernova with the naked eye, a historic astronomical event that revolutionized understanding of the cosmos. This naked-eye supernova challenged the prevailing belief that the heavens were immutable.

articles.title: Giant exoplanet emerges from the dark when the James Webb Space Telescope turns out the starlight
articles.description: Astronomers have filtered out starlight from James Webb Space Telescope observations to see a giant exoplanet emerge in the darkness.
articles.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope has successfully filtered out starlight to directly image a giant exoplanet in its system. This breakthrough technique advances our ability to study distant worlds and search for potentially habitable environments.

articles.title: Hera probe gets 1st good look at asteroid system clobbered by NASA's DART mission | Space photo of the day for Nov. 6, 2026
articles.description: The European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft has gotten its first close-up look at the Didymos binary asteroid, the first space rock system "punched" by humanity.
articles.summary: The European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft has obtained its first close-up observations of the Didymos binary asteroid, target of NASA's historic DART planetary defense mission. This follow-up study validates humanity's first test of asteroid deflection technology.

articles.title: Physicists step closer to the 'Zeptoverse' after 42-year particle search
articles.description: Physicists have found evidence of a particle decay so rare that it is expected to occur only around once in every 10 billion "beauty" particles. The result, from the upgraded LHCb experiment at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC), follows a search spanning mor…
articles.summary: Physicists have discovered evidence of an extraordinarily rare particle decay after a 42-year search, occurring roughly once per 10 billion events. This breakthrough expands our understanding of fundamental physics and the exotic particles that shape our universe.

articles.title: Nanohertz Gravitational-Wave Constraints on Supermassive Binary Black Holes at Cosmic Dawn
articles.description: Author(s): Yiqin Chen, Shi-Yi Zhao, Xingjiang Zhu, N. D. Ramesh Bhat, Jacob Cardinal Tremblay, Małgorzata Curyło, Valentina Di Marco, George Hobbs, Wenhua Ling, Rami F. Mandow, Richard N. Manchester, Saurav Mishra, Daniel J. Reardon, Sparrow Roch, Christopher…
articles.summary: New research using nanohertz gravitational-wave observations constrains the properties of supermassive binary black holes at cosmic dawn. These findings deepen our understanding of black hole formation and merger dynamics in the early universe.

articles.title: Two Different Kinds of Gamma-Ray Bursts Erupted 4 Minutes Apart. Astronomers Have Never Seen This Before.
articles.description: Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are among the most energetic cosmic events since the Big Bang, releasing the most energetic type of radiation, gamma rays – the stuff that turned unassuming Bruce Banner into the rampaging Hulk, but on an astronomical, potentially plan…
articles.summary: Astronomers observed two different types of gamma-ray bursts erupting just 4 minutes apart, a phenomenon never before witnessed. This rare cosmic event provides new insights into some of the universe's most energetic explosions.

articles.title: Figuring out where cosmic neutrinos come from is tricky - radio telescopes could help find where these ‘ghost particles’ originate
articles.description: A researcher just won a Nobel Prize for detecting tiny particles from space. Scientists now want to get better at figuring out where in the cosmos they come from.
articles.summary: Scientists are developing radio telescope technology to better detect and locate cosmic neutrinos, building on recent Nobel Prize-winning detection work. This advancement will help unlock the origins of these elusive 'ghost particles' from space.

articles.title: Possible dwarf planet discovered beyond Pluto
articles.description: Astronomers have found a large icy object beyond Pluto, dubbed 2026 ED138, that could become the solar system’s sixth dwarf planet Read Full Article at RT.com
articles.summary: Astronomers have discovered a large icy object beyond Pluto designated 2026 ED138 that may qualify as the solar system's sixth dwarf planet. This finding expands our understanding of the outer solar system's composition.

articles.title: Ein Lichttag entfernt: Voyager 1 soll neue Rekordmarke überschreiten
articles.description: Die Raumsonde Voyager 1 soll am 18. November exakt einen Licht­tag von unserem Planeten entfernt sein. Ein simpler Befehl benötigt dann 24 Stunden bis zur Ankunft. Wie lange hält die schwindende Energiequelle der fast 50 Jahre alten Technik noch durch?(Weiter…
articles.summary: Voyager 1 is approaching a historic milestone, reaching a distance of exactly one light-day from Earth on November 18th. This remarkable achievement underscores humanity's greatest deep space exploration accomplishment.

articles.summary: Hubble captures a silhouetted view of Saturn's moon Enceladus, revealing the dramatic interplay of light and shadow in our solar system.

articles.title: Earth's Gravity May Have Kept the Early Moon's Volcanic Heart Beating
articles.description: We typically think of the Moon as a static, floating object that has remained the same for basically its entire lifetime, with an occasional asteroid impact serving as an exception. That understanding is grounded in physics - the Moon should have cooled rapidly after forming when a huge protoplanet hit the early Earth around 4.5 billion years ago. But, some lunar material returned from the Chang’e-5 mission was notably formed only around two billion years ago, yet appeared to be volcanic in origin. So how did a world that was supposed to have settled down without volcanism remain hot enough to create these materials more than two billion years after its violent birth? A new paper from Miao Chen of the Chengdu University of Technology and his colleagues, and recently published in the journal Planet, offers an explanation - tidal heating.
articles.summary: New research reveals that Earth's gravity may have sustained the Moon's volcanic activity in its early history, reshaping our understanding of lunar evolution.

articles.title: Asteroids' Oddball Shapes Make Deflecting Them Challenging
articles.description: In a pinch, we could use a stand-off nuclear blast to redirect a dangerous asteroid on short notice. There's no atmospheric shock wave in space, but the x-ray pulse could still deflect the space rock. But asteroids aren't round and uniform, so their weird shapes make it difficult.
articles.summary: Scientists explore the challenges of deflecting asteroids by studying their oddball shapes and developing innovative planetary defense strategies.
